title: Even Parity Bit
statement:
Compute the even-parity bit for an 8-bit value: the single bit that, added
to the data, makes the total number of `1` bits even.

## Your entity

```
entity solution is
    port (
        data   : in  std_logic_vector(7 downto 0);
        parity : out std_logic
    );
end entity solution;
```

`data(7)` is the eight bits to check; `parity` is `'1'` when `data` itself
holds an *odd* number of ones (so adding the parity bit brings the total to
an even number), `'0'` when `data` already holds an even number.

`"10110001"` has four ones -- already even -- so `parity` is `'0'`.
`"10110000"` has three -- odd -- so `parity` is `'1'`.

## Input and output

The testbench reads one line of stdin as an 8-character bit string, drives
it onto `data`, waits for the output to settle, and writes `parity` back out
as a single `'0'` or `'1'` character.

## Watch out

- The direct definition -- XOR every bit together, in order -- is also the
  simplest circuit for this: `xor` is one of the handful of VHDL-2008
  operators with a *reduction* form, so `xor data` (no loop, no index) folds
  an entire `std_logic_vector` down to one bit. Writing out `data(7) xor
  data(6) xor ...` by hand is not wrong, just eight symbols longer and one
  more place to drop a bit.

tests.name: all zero
tests.description: Zero ones -- already even, so no parity bit is needed.

tests.name: all ones
tests.description: Eight ones is even, the same as all-zero -- a solution that special-cases 0 without actually computing the parity would get this one wrong.

tests.name: seven ones
tests.description: Odd count from a run of ones rather than a single scattered bit.
